title: Themistocles Sends a Secret Message
text:
In September 480 BC the Greek fleet lay at Salamis, near Athens, which the Persians had just burned. Many Greek commanders wanted to sail back to the Isthmus of Corinth to defend the Peloponnese. Themistocles of Athens believed the only chance was to fight in the narrow strait, where the larger Persian fleet could not use its numbers. He was losing the argument.

Herodotus tells how he forced the issue. He slipped out of the council and sent his trusted slave Sicinnus, the tutor of his children, by boat to the Persian camp. Sicinnus told the Persian commanders that Themistocles secretly favored the king, that the Greeks were terrified and about to flee, and that if the Persians attacked now the Greeks would fight each other instead of them.

Xerxes believed it. During the night Persian ships moved to block both exits from the strait. When the Greek captains learned that they were surrounded, the debate was over: they had to fight where they were.

The next day the Persian ships, crowded in the narrows, fouled each other and were badly beaten while Xerxes watched from the shore. Soon after, he withdrew with much of his army to Asia. Herodotus adds that Themistocles later made Sicinnus a citizen of Thespiae and a rich man.
lesson: Choosing the ground of a contest can matter more than the size of the forces. Sometimes you must arrange the situation so that the right decision is the only one left.
source: Herodotus, Histories 8.75 to 8.96; Plutarch, Life of Themistocles 12
